items.title: How a DomainException becomes an HTTP response
items.body:
`ExceptionHandlingMiddleware` wraps the whole request: `try { await _next(context); }`. If a `DomainException` is thrown anywhere below, the `catch (DomainException exception)` arm calls `WriteProblemAsync` with the exception's own status code, code and message. That method sets the content type to `application/problem+json`, builds a `ProblemDetails` object, and adds two extensions: `code` and `traceId`. So the client gets the right status plus a machine-readable code and an id to quote when reporting the error. Other exceptions get a generic 500, with details hidden outside Development.

Why the others are wrong:
- The developer exception page is not what writes these responses; the custom middleware is.
- The endpoints have no try/catch; they just call the service.
- There is no result-wrapper type; errors travel as exceptions to the middleware.

excerpts.quote: catch (DomainException exception) { await WriteProblemAsync(context, exception.StatusCode, exception.Code, exception.Message); }
context.Response.StatusCode = statusCode; context.Response.ContentType = "application/problem+json";
problem.Extensions["code"] = code; problem.Extensions["traceId"] = Activity.Current?.Id ?? context.TraceIdentifier;

items.title: Why changing a board from GetAsync cannot corrupt the store
items.body:
`GetAsync` never returns the stored object. It returns `stored.Clone()`. `Board.Clone` creates a new Board, and the Board constructor copies each column with `column.Clone()`; each column in turn copies its cards with `card.Clone()`. So the caller gets a deep, detached copy. Calling mutators on it only changes that copy. The only way to change stored data is through `UpdateAsync`, which also works on a clone and stores a clone. The stored objects never leave the repository.

Why the others are wrong:
- `GetAsync` does not take the write lock; it does not need to, since it hands out a copy.
- It is safe, precisely because of the clone.
- Board has mutator methods that change it in place; it is not an immutable record. Safety comes from copying.

excerpts.quote: public Task<Board?> GetAsync(Guid boardId, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); var board = _boards.TryGetValue(boardId, out var stored) ? stored.Clone() : null; return Task.FromResult(board);
_columns = columns?.OrderBy(column => column.Position).Select(column => column.Clone()).ToList() ?? [];
_cards = cards?.OrderBy(card => card.Position).Select(card => card.Clone()).ToList() ?? [];

items.title: What a card limit of 0 means
items.body:
`EnsureCardLimit` runs after a card is added. It throws only when `CardLimit > 0 && _cards.Count > CardLimit`. If `CardLimit` is 0, the first condition is false, so the whole check is skipped and any number of cards is allowed. So 0 is used to mean "no limit" for Backlog and Done, while In progress, with limit 4, throws `DomainException.Conflict("column.card_limit", ...)` when a fifth card arrives.

Why the others are wrong:
- A 0-limit column accepts cards; the check is skipped, not triggered.
- Nothing rejects or changes 0 when a column is created.
- There is no board-wide default limit in this code.

excerpts.quote: private void EnsureCardLimit() { if (CardLimit > 0 && _cards.Count > CardLimit) { throw DomainException.Conflict("column.card_limit", $"Column '{Title}' allows at most {CardLimit} cards."); } }
public void AddCard(Card card) { _cards.Insert(Math.Clamp(card.Position, 0, _cards.Count), card); EnsureCardLimit(); ReindexCards();

items.title: Why an unknown assignee id gets 400 member.not_found
items.body:
When a card is created with an assignee, the board runs `EnsureAssigneeExists`. A null assignee is fine (the method returns at once). Otherwise, if `_members.All(member => member.Id != assigneeId.Value)` (no member has that id), it throws `DomainException.BadRequest("member.not_found", "Assignee is not a member of this board.")`. The middleware turns this into a 400. A well-formed GUID is not enough; it has to be one of the board's members.

Why the others are wrong:
- Membership *is* checked, so it is not 201.
- The board exists and the request is invalid, so it is a 400 bad request, not a 404.
- Nothing about the member list is versioned or compared, so no 409.

excerpts.quote: private void EnsureAssigneeExists(Guid? assigneeId) { if (assigneeId is null) { return; } if (_members.All(member => member.Id != assigneeId.Value)) { throw DomainException.BadRequest("member.not_found", "Assignee is not a member of this board."); }

items.title: What "archiving" a card really does
items.body:
The DELETE route calls `ArchiveCardAsync`, which ends in `Board.ArchiveCard`. That method finds the card's column, calls `sourceColumn.RemoveCard(cardId)`, and updates the board's timestamp. Nothing keeps the removed card: no archive column, no flag, no file. The card object is simply dropped, so the action is a permanent delete. The name "archive" promises more than the code does, which is worth raising in a review.

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no hidden Archive column.
- Nothing writes the card to disk; storage is in memory anyway.
- There is no `IsArchived` flag set; the card is removed from the list.

excerpts.quote: public void ArchiveCard(Guid cardId, DateTimeOffset now) { var sourceColumn = FindColumnContainingCard(cardId); sourceColumn.RemoveCard(cardId); Touch(now); }

boards.MapDelete("/{boardId:guid}/cards/{cardId:guid}", async (Guid boardId, Guid cardId, HttpRequest httpRequest, BoardService service, CancellationToken cancellationToken) => Results.Ok(await service.ArchiveCardAsync(boardId, cardId, ReadExpectedVersion(httpRequest), cancellationToken)));

items.title: Exactly when board.version_conflict is thrown
items.body:
Inside the repository's update, `MutateAsync` checks `if (expectedVersion is not null && board.Version != expectedVersion.Value)` and throws `DomainException.Conflict("board.version_conflict", ...)`. Both parts must be true: the client sent a version (the header was present, so `ReadExpectedVersion` did not return null), **and** it differs from the stored board's version. If the header is missing, `expectedVersion` is null and the check is skipped entirely. The critique flags this opt-in design as a risk: clients that never send the header get last-write-wins.

Why the others are wrong:
- A missing header does not fail; it skips the check.
- The version comes from the `X-Board-Version` header, not from the request body.
- Two racing requests without headers both skip the check; nothing throws.

excerpts.quote: if (expectedVersion is not null && board.Version != expectedVersion.Value) { throw DomainException.Conflict("board.version_conflict", "The board changed since it was last loaded. Refresh and try again."); }
if (!request.Headers.TryGetValue("X-Board-Version", out var value)) { return null; }

items.title: What a caller must prove before editing a card: nothing
items.body:
The validation-and-permissions guide is direct: "No authentication or authorization code was found." The endpoints in `BoardEndpoints.cs` do not call `RequireAuthorization`, do not use `[Authorize]`, and never check who the caller is. Look at the PATCH route: it takes the board id, card id, body and headers and calls the service. Board "members" exist only as display data in the seed, not as security principals. So anyone who can reach the API can PATCH any card.

Why the others are wrong:
- The version header is a concurrency check, not a secret. It is a number the API hands out with every board.
- There is no session or CSRF code in the server.
- `EnsureAssigneeExists` checks that an *assignee* is on the board's member list. The guide calls treating it as authorization a "junior miss"; it says nothing about the caller.

excerpts.quote: No authentication or authorization code was found. Endpoints in `src/NetTrello.Api/Endpoints/BoardEndpoints.cs:11-41` do not call `RequireAuthorization`, use `[Authorize]`, or check user identity. Members currently exist as display data in seed storage (`src/NetTrello.Api/Infrastructure/InMemoryBoardRepository.cs:15-22`), not as security principals.

boards.MapPatch("/{boardId:guid}/cards/{cardId:guid}", async (Guid boardId, Guid cardId, UpdateCardRequest request, HttpRequest httpRequest, BoardService service, CancellationToken cancellationToken) => Results.Ok(await service.UpdateCardAsync(boardId, cardId, request, ReadExpectedVersion(httpRequest), cancellationToken)));

- Junior miss: "Assignee check is authorization." Senior check: `EnsureAssigneeExists` only validates display membership at `src/NetTrello.Api/Domain/Board.cs:113-123`; it does not prove the caller can edit the board.

items.title: Start here: NetTrello and its upskill lab
items.body:
NetTrello is a small Trello-style app: boards contain columns, columns contain cards. There is one ASP.NET Core minimal API project under `src/NetTrello.Api/` and a Vite React client under `client/`. Boards are kept in memory, not in a database.

Read in this order:

- **docs/upskill/README.md**: the one-paragraph map of where everything starts, and how to use the lab.
- **01-codebase-cartography/01-system-map.md**: the project graph, runtime boundaries and the "Ownership Rules" (which file owns which job).
- **01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md**: each flow traced through the code: load a board, create a board, add a card, move a card with optimistic concurrency, edit and archive, errors.
- **03-architecture-and-patterns/**: data model and persistence, validation and permissions, and the architecture critique.
- **08-reference/risk-register.md**: the known risks in one table.

Most quizzes are about code in `Domain/Board.cs`, `Domain/BoardColumn.cs`, `Endpoints/BoardEndpoints.cs` and `Infrastructure/InMemoryBoardRepository.cs`. Read the method the quiz names line by line.

excerpts.quote: NetTrello is a compact Trello-style training repo with one ASP.NET Core API project and one Vite React client.
- Components render and gather form input; see `client/src/components/CardEditor.tsx:22-35` and `client/src/components/CardComposer.tsx:18-35`.

readMore.why: Every main flow traced through the code.

items.title: Why moving a column to position 999 puts it last
items.body:
`MoveColumn` removes the column from the list and inserts it again at `Math.Clamp(position, 0, _columns.Count)`. Clamp forces a number into a range: anything above the top becomes the top. With the column removed, three remain, so 999 becomes 3, the end of the list. Then `ReindexColumns` walks the list and sets each column's position to its index (0, 1, 2, 3), so there are no gaps. An out-of-range position is corrected, not rejected.

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no range validation that returns 400 here; the value is clamped.
- A large position has nothing to do with a stale version, so no 409.
- Reindexing rewrites every position, so 999 is never stored.

excerpts.quote: public void MoveColumn(Guid columnId, int position, DateTimeOffset now) { var column = FindColumn(columnId); _columns.Remove(column); _columns.Insert(Math.Clamp(position, 0, _columns.Count), column); ReindexColumns(); Touch(now);
private void ReindexColumns() { for (var index = 0; index < _columns.Count; index++) { _columns[index].MoveTo(index); } }

items.title: Why a failed card move never leaves a card missing
items.body:
`MoveCard` really does remove the card from its source column first, and `AddCard` on the target can then throw if the column is full. What protects the stored board is the repository. `UpdateAsync` does `var updated = update(existing.Clone());`: the update runs on a **copy**. Only on the next line, `_boards[boardId] = updated.Clone();`, is the result stored. If the update throws, that line never runs; the exception leaves the method and the half-changed copy is simply thrown away. The stored board is still the last good version.

Why the others are wrong:
- The limit check runs inside `AddCard`, after the removal, so the move *can* throw midway.
- There is no compensating catch that re-inserts the card.
- The lock only makes updates take turns; it does not roll anything back. The clone is what does.

excerpts.quote: var updated = update(existing.Clone()); _boards[boardId] = updated.Clone(); return updated.Clone();
var sourceColumn = FindColumnContainingCard(cardId); var card = sourceColumn.RemoveCard(cardId); card.MoveTo(position, now); var targetColumn = FindColumn(targetColumnId); targetColumn.AddCard(card);

items.title: What happens when X-Board-Version is not a number
items.body:
`ReadExpectedVersion` handles three cases. No header at all: it returns `null` and the version check is skipped. A header that parses as an integer: it returns that number. A header that is present but not an integer, like "abc": `int.TryParse` returns false and the code throws `DomainException.BadRequest("board.version_invalid", "X-Board-Version must be an integer.")`. The middleware turns that into a 400 with code `board.version_invalid`. The mutation never runs.

Why the others are wrong:
- The value is rejected while parsing, before any comparison with the board's version, so no 409.
- A present header is never ignored; only an *absent* one leads to null.
- The code uses `TryParse`, which does not throw, so there is no unhandled 500.

excerpts.quote: private static int? ReadExpectedVersion(HttpRequest request) { if (!request.Headers.TryGetValue("X-Board-Version", out var value)) { return null; } if (!int.TryParse(value, out var version)) { throw DomainException.BadRequest("board.version_invalid", "X-Board-Version must be an integer."); } return version;

items.title: Concept: endpoint, service, domain object, repository
items.body:
The system map's "Ownership Rules" say who is responsible for what on the server:

- **Endpoints** (`BoardEndpoints.cs`) map URLs to service calls and read request headers.
- **`BoardService`** owns the order of steps for each use case and the optimistic concurrency check (the board's version number).
- **Domain objects** (`Board`, `BoardColumn`, `Card`) own the rules, called *invariants*, and all state changes. When a rule is broken they throw a `DomainException` carrying an HTTP status and an error code.
- **The repository** stores boards. Here it is in memory, behind the `IBoardRepository` interface so it could be replaced.
- **Middleware** turns exceptions into HTTP responses.

This tells you where to look. "Is this input accepted?" is usually answered in a domain method. "Which status code comes back?" depends on which exception is thrown and how the middleware writes it. "Can stored data end up half-changed?" is a question about the repository.

excerpts.quote: - `BoardService` owns use-case sequencing and optimistic concurrency; see `src/NetTrello.Api/Application/BoardService.cs:106-119`. - Domain objects own invariants and state mutation; see `src/NetTrello.Api/Domain/Board.cs:113-156`.
| Persistence | In-memory repository | `src/NetTrello.Api/Infrastructure/InMemoryBoardRepository.cs:7-85` | Replaceable infrastructure |

items.title: Concept: board versions and problem+json errors
items.body:
Two cross-cutting ideas appear in many quizzes.

**Board versions.** Every board has a `Version` number that grows with each change. A client can send the version it last saw in an `X-Board-Version` request header. The service compares it with the stored board before changing anything, so a client working from an old copy can be told to refresh instead of silently overwriting someone else's change. The key-flows doc traces this in "Move Card With Optimistic Concurrency".

**Errors as data.** Domain code throws a `DomainException` with a status (400, 404, 409...) and a short machine-readable code such as `board.not_found`. The API turns errors into a standard JSON shape called *problem details* (`application/problem+json`), so the client can show the message and act on the code.

When a quiz asks for an outcome, give both parts: the status, and the code string from the `throw` line.

excerpts.quote: **Why it matters:** This is the most important production idea in the repo: prevent stale browser state from silently overwriting another change.
**Why it matters:** Production systems need stable failure shapes so clients can respond without parsing random strings.
